The first rescue should feel genuinely good to pull off. The unease comes in quietly, in a detail nobody's had time to check.
chapters.dmNote: Play this tier almost entirely straight. The four of them are good at this, the agency needs them, and the town is grateful in a way U.A.'s campus never quite was — that's a real and earned feeling, let it land before anything complicates it. The sinkhole's clean edges are the only thread pulling forward; everything else is character work and competence porn.

sections.heading: Orientation Day
sections.readAloud: The bus from the last train station lets you off outside a converted hardware store with a hand-painted sign reading TIDEWELL POINT AGENCY — EST. hanging slightly crooked above the door. The street behind you is one block long. It has a noodle shop, a shuttered bank branch, and a memorial plaque bolted to a boulder that you will learn not to ask about on day one.
sections.body:
• Amagai meets you at the door, looks at all four of you for slightly too long, and says "Four. Huh." before showing you the back room that is now your office, equipment locker, and — per the cot in the corner — occasional crash space.
• Sesshin is warmer, immediately curious about all four quirks in a genuinely nerdy way, and asks Izuto detailed questions about Engine's fluid-replenishment math that Izuto is delighted to answer at length.
• Amagai's actual onboarding speech is four sentences long: "Nobody's coming to back you up. Call it in anyway, every time, even when you don't need it, so dispatch has a pattern. Don't be a hero. Be useful." She does not explain further.
• Paperwork, gear checks, and a driving tour of the town's known soft zones — marked on a laminated map that is visibly older than the agency's coffee maker.
• Local color: Ren's U.A. reputation means nothing here, which he finds bizarrely more unsettling than being recognized would be. Kazama is immediately liked by the noodle shop owner, who starts sending food to the agency unprompted within the week. Izuto reorganizes the equipment locker on day two without being asked and it takes Sesshin four days to notice, at which point he's mostly just impressed. Chozen has already produced a one-page contingency summary for "agency loses power during active rescue" that nobody requested and Amagai pins to the corkboard without comment, which Chozen correctly reads as the highest compliment she's capable of giving.
sections.dmNote: This section has no combat. Its job is to establish four things fast: the town is small and specific, the agency is two tired professionals doing more than two people should, the class hierarchy that mattered at U.A. means nothing here, and each PC gets one unforced character beat before anything goes wrong. Let players improvise their own version of "the town notices them" — Kazama's kindness and Izuto's competence tend to land immediately; Ren and Chozen take a little longer to be read correctly by people who don't know them yet.

sections.heading: First Call: The Kessler Street Sinkhole
sections.readAloud: The alarm comes in on your third day. Kessler Street — the one with the memorial boulder — has opened up outside the bank branch that's been closed for six years. Ground floor's gone into the hole; the second floor is folded down at an angle that shouldn't be structurally possible and currently is. There's a shopkeeper from next door who ran in to grab the cash box before anyone told her not to. She's on what's left of the second floor. It's still settling.
sections.body:
• Amagai anchors the boulevard's remaining edge with Ballast and gets exactly one clear sentence out before she's fully committed to holding it: "Get her, don't touch the middle, go."
• The floor is actively unstable — treat it as difficult, hazardous terrain that can collapse further on a bad roll or a heavy hit. This is the first chance to show off: Kazama can plant himself as a physical brace point for the others to work off of; Izuto's Engine lets him cross the unstable middle fast enough that his weight barely registers before he's past it; Ren gets there fastest and has to actually slow down and think for once, because speed alone doesn't solve "the floor gives way under her the second you grab her arm."
• Chozen's Stress should start climbing here for real — this is live, worsening, physically demanding danger, not sparring. Let his bonuses kick in mid-rescue and have him notice it happening, matter-of-fact rather than dramatic.
• Secondary collapse: partway through, a support somewhere below groans audibly. This is the moment to test whether the party works as a unit or four individuals — Kazama holding a beam, Izuto scouting the safest path, Ren making the actual carry, Chozen doing the unglamorous work of stabilizing rubble so the other three have somewhere to stand.
• The shopkeeper is fine. Shaken, extremely apologetic, already asking if the cash box survived (it did not; she does not seem to actually care that much once she says it out loud).
sections.dmNote: This is the party's proof-of-concept encounter — first time working together, first time the town watches them do it. Nobody needs to almost die. What matters is that it's harder than an exam scenario: real weight, real consequences, no do-overs. Give each PC one clean mechanical spotlight moment per the beats above. End on a genuinely warm beat — Amagai's assessment afterward should be a single unimpressed sentence that is nonetheless the nicest thing she's said all week.

aside.label: Something Off
aside.body: DC 14 Investigation (or Intelligence/Nature check with a relevant background) during or after the rescue notices the sinkhole's edges are unusually clean — sheared rather than crumbled, like something cut a line rather than the ground simply giving way. Amagai clocks a player noticing this and says only, "Yeah. Log it," and doesn't elaborate. She's noticed the same thing on the last two.

sections.heading: Small Town, Long Memory
sections.readAloud: The noodle shop, evening, the day after the rescue. It's the kind of place where four strangers eating together get noticed, and get talked to.
sections.body:
• Locals are grateful, and also unsentimental about it: more than one person mentions, without much heat, that heroes weren't around for the Ashfall and the mining company's lawyers were faster than any rescue team. This isn't hostility. It's just what's true here.
• An older man — regulars call him Denbei, doesn't offer a last name — mentions he worked the seam for twenty-two years and lost his younger brother in the collapse. He says the settlement money "bought exactly one new roof and a lot of nothing," states it as fact rather than a grievance, and changes the subject before anyone can turn it into a moment.
• Someone mentions, half-joking, that the ground's been "grumpier" than usual this year — three incidents instead of the usual one every year or two — and the table generally agrees without treating it as significant.
• This is the party's first unforced exposure to the town's relationship with the disaster: tired, specific, and not asking to be rescued from the memory of it. Nobody here is a villain and nobody here is asking the party to fix anything except the actual, physical, current problem.
sections.dmNote: Plant Denbei clearly enough that his name means something later, but do not signal him as important — he's one of a dozen people saying similar things tonight, not a spotlighted NPC yet. The goal of this scene is sympathy for the town's grievance in the abstract, well before the party has any reason to connect it to anything happening now.

closing.label: Chapter Note — Frequency
closing.body: Three incidents in ten weeks against a historical rate of one every year or two is roughly a ten-times acceleration. Nobody has said this number out loud yet. Amagai will, eventually, once she trusts the party enough to say it in front of them instead of just frowning at the corkboard.

chapters.title: Aftershocks
chapters.intro: The competence-porn rescue arc gets a second, harder layer: the accidents aren't accidents, the mining company is managing a liability problem instead of a safety one, and the evidence keeps pointing somewhere the party will recognize before the story says it outright. This tier is about the ground rules changing under a job the party thought they already understood.
chapters.dmNote: Let the players get ahead of the reveal if they're paying attention — Denbei was introduced warmly in Chapter 1 specifically so that recognizing him here lands as dread, not a twist for its own sake. This tier should feel heavier than Chapter 1 without losing the grounded, procedural rescue-work tone; the danger is realer, not more theatrical.

sections.heading: The Company Man
sections.readAloud: A rental car with city plates parks outside the agency on a Tuesday. The man who gets out introduces himself as Sato from Kessler Mining's "regional liaison office" — a division that, as far as anyone in the Hollow knew, closed in 2019. He wants to talk about "recent subsidence events" and whether the agency's incident reports have been "appropriately categorized."
sections.body:
• Sato is polite, unhurried, and extremely interested in whether Tidewell Point's official reports use the word "anomalous" anywhere. They do not — Amagai's writing is dry to the point of self-defense, and she's noticed him noticing that.
• He offers, almost as an aside, a modest "community goodwill fund" contribution to the agency's equipment budget — timed suspiciously close to this conversation. Amagai has not yet said no. She also hasn't cashed anything.
• Pressed (DC 15 Persuasion or Insight to get past his script), Sato lets slip that Kessler Mining maintains a private structural monitoring contract on the old workings — meaning someone has better data on the tunnels than the town does, and has for years, and never shared it.
• He leaves his card. He does not leave a straight answer to "why does a closed regional office need to know if we're using the word anomalous."
sections.dmNote: Sato isn't the villain and shouldn't play like one — he's a company employee managing liability exposure, competent and a little bored by it. His usefulness is entirely as a lead: the mining company has data the party doesn't, and is actively managing the story rather than the ground. Let the party's read on him be "slimy but probably not directly dangerous," which is correct.

sections.heading: Under Miller's Ridge
sections.readAloud: The call comes in at 6am: a maintenance crew doing routine work in the old Miller's Ridge access tunnel — the one Kessler Mining supposedly sealed in 2019 — didn't check in for their scheduled radio contact. Amagai's face when dispatch says "Miller's Ridge" is the first time any of you have seen her look actually rattled.
sections.body:
• The tunnel wasn't fully sealed — a maintenance sub-contractor has apparently been quietly using it for storage access for years, unlogged, which is its own small scandal nobody has time for right now.
• A partial collapse has trapped a four-person crew roughly 200 meters in, in a section with a compromised support beam and a slow gas seep that makes open flame and heavy percussive impacts actively dangerous.
• This is the tier's core structural-collapse showcase and should run over multiple scenes: Izuto scouting the safest route through debris and gas pockets using Engine's speed and his own tactical read of the space; Kazama physically bracing a failing support beam long enough for extraction, at real cost to his daily Steel uses; Ren making repeated fast extraction runs, each one riskier as the tunnel destabilizes further; Chozen's Stress climbing hard and staying up as the situation refuses to resolve cleanly, giving him real escalating output right when the party needs it most.
• Mid-rescue, someone (ideally Izuto, scouting ahead) can make a DC 16 Perception check and notice fresh charge-scoring on one section of support timber — small, deliberate, recent. Not old mine damage. This is the first hard evidence the collapses are being caused, not just accelerating naturally.
• All four crew members survive if the party works the encounter as written. If the party is careless or unlucky, let one crew member be seriously hurt rather than killed — this campaign is grim at the edges, not cruel to its NPCs by default.
sections.dmNote: This is the tier's spotlight sequence — give it real time and let every PC's kit matter distinctly rather than resolving through one dominant strategy. Chozen should end this scene visibly wrung out but at genuine peak output; this is a good moment to remind the table that his escalation doesn't come free. Izuto finding the evidence personally (rather than it being handed to the party) matters for his arc — he's the one who insists on checking one more thing instead of calling it done, which is very in-character and worth spotlighting.

aside.label: Evidence
aside.body: The scored timber is deliberate demolition charge residue, old-fashioned and analog rather than quirk-based — someone wanted this to look natural and mostly succeeded. A DC 14 Investigation check on the char pattern gives a rough age estimate: roughly two weeks old, which lines up with incident #3, not today's collapse. Today's collapse looks, on first pass, actually natural. That inconsistency is the hook forward.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.readAloud: Back at the agency, corkboard covered in incident dates, survey maps, and Chozen's increasingly detailed handwriting, the pattern starts to resolve if anyone sits down and actually looks for it.
sections.body:
• Cross-referencing incident dates against the mining company's old employee records (which Amagai has, in a filing cabinet, because she's been here longer than the company's given her credit for) turns up a pattern: every incident site is within a hundred meters of where a named miner died in the original Ashfall.
• Denbei's brother's name is on that list. So are two others. So, unnervingly, is a fourth location that hasn't had an incident yet — which becomes the obvious next move if the party is thinking ahead rather than reacting.
• A DC 15 Streetwise or Insight check around town turns up that Denbei has been "different" the last year or so — more private, doing something with his evenings nobody's quite placed, seen out near Miller's Ridge more than a hobby explains.
• The party does not need to "solve" this scene with a single roll — let it be a genuine table discussion about what the pattern means and who to talk to first. If they go straight to Denbei, that's correct and the campaign is built to support it.
sections.dmNote: This scene exists to let the players do the detective work rather than have it handed down, and to make the eventual reveal feel earned rather than sprung. If your table is moving slowly or stuck, Sesshin can nudge them — he's a genuinely good listener and has picked up more town gossip than he realizes is relevant.

closing.label: Chapter Note — The Fourth Site
closing.body: The pattern points to one more location that hasn't had an incident yet: the sealed mouth of the original collapse shaft, up on the ridge above the old company offices. If the party doesn't get there first, Chapter 3 opens with the sequence beginning anyway, worse and further along.

chapters.title: Undermine
chapters.intro: The finale trades scale for intimacy — one grieving, furious, precise man against everything the party has learned to be good at, on ground that was never stable to begin with. This is a campaign about infrastructure and negligence and the people left holding both, and the ending should feel earned rather than triumphant.
chapters.dmNote: Resist the urge to make Denbei bigger, stranger, or more powerful than a person with an unregistered, narrow, patient Quirk and twenty years of motive. The horror here is scale, not power level — a genuinely dangerous encounter built from ordinary physics and one very tired man, exactly the kind of threat this specific party (structural, rescue-capable, self-sufficient) was matched to the Hollow to handle.

sections.heading: The Man Who Wouldn't Leave
sections.readAloud: The old shaft mouth on the ridge is caged off and rusted, and someone has clearly been coming here regularly — a worn path through the brush, a folding chair, a thermos. Denbei is here, not hiding, sitting with his back to the cage like he's been waiting.
sections.body:
• Denbei doesn't run and doesn't lie once confronted with what the party's found. His Quirk — never registered, never used publicly in twenty years of mining work because a working man with a destabilization Quirk doesn't get hired twice — is Faultline: he can weaken stone and packed earth's cohesion at a distance, sense-and-destabilize rather than move it outright. He used it exactly the way the settlement lawyers used their paperwork: precisely, and where it would be believed as natural.
• His case, delivered plainly rather than as a villain speech: Kessler Mining's private monitoring data — the data Sato all but confirmed exists — has apparently shown accelerating instability for years and been quietly filed as an internal liability number instead of a public safety issue. He can't prove that in court. He also has a Quirk built exactly for making the ground itself say what the paperwork won't.
• He is careful to say, and clearly means, that he never intended anyone to actually get hurt — the timing and locations were chosen around maintenance schedules and known-empty structures. Miller's Ridge, with a live crew inside on unscheduled work, scared him too. That's true, and it's also exactly why an angry, careful man's plan was always going to eventually hurt someone.
• Give the party a real choice point here: talk him down, try to arrest him outright, or let him make his case somewhere it might actually matter (the Commission, a journalist, Amagai directly). All three are legitimate table outcomes and the DM notes below cover branching from here.
sections.dmNote: Denbei should never feel evil. He should feel like someone the table likes, whose method they can't endorse, in a situation the actual system failed to resolve honestly. This is the emotional peak of the campaign — let it breathe. If the table tries to talk him down, that's a full scene, not a skip-to-combat. If he panics or feels cornered, that's what triggers Collapse Point, not villain monologuing.

aside.label: If The Party Talked Him Down
aside.body: Skip straight to Collapse Point's aftermath: Denbei surrenders, the shaft is unstable anyway from twenty years of accumulated damage he can no longer fully control even if he wanted to stop, and the party still has to get everyone off the ridge before it goes. The confrontation becomes a rescue instead of a fight — arguably more in-genre for this table's skill set.

sections.heading: Collapse Point
sections.readAloud: Whatever brought this to a head — a panicked reaction, a refusal to stand down, or simply the ridge finally giving out on its own twenty-year clock — the ground under the old shaft mouth is failing in real time, and it is bigger than anything the party has handled so far.
sections.body:
• This is not a fight against Denbei so much as a fight against the mountain, with Denbei as a variable inside it — his Quirk is actively making things worse even if he's trying to stop, because Faultline doesn't have a clean off switch once a fracture network is already running.
• Structure the encounter as an escalating, multi-stage rescue-under-fire: the ridge access road is failing behind them (retreat route closing), the shaft mouth itself is venting unstable gas, and there may be one or two of Sato's mining-company "private security" contractors on-site (there to quietly monitor the site, now very out of their depth) who need extracting whether the party likes them or not.
• Spotlight moment for Chozen: this is the scenario his contingency binder has no page for. Let his Stress hit genuine peak output here, and let the DM notes' growth arc pay off — he improvises without a plan for the first time, out loud, in front of the team.
• Spotlight moment for Izuto: at some point his best read of the situation requires trusting someone else's judgment over his own — asking Kazama to hold a line Izuto can't personally verify is safe, or asking Ren to make a call Izuto isn't fast enough to make himself. Let him actually ask.
• Spotlight moment for Ren: give him one beat where the joke doesn't land — where speed gets someone almost-but-not-quite in time, and the sarcasm runs out for a second before he does the actually brave thing anyway.
• Spotlight moment for Kazama: if his scar has never come up, this is the natural place — a moment structurally identical to whatever it is he didn't act on before, except this time he does, immediately, without the hesitation the scar represents.
• Denbei's fate depends on the table: he can go down trying to undo what he started (redemptive), get pulled out alongside everyone else and face what's coming (arrested, sympathetic), or — if things go worst — not make it out, in which case let his last act be trying to stabilize the section the party's still in rather than saving himself.
sections.dmNote: This encounter should feel like the hardest thing the party has done, mechanically and emotionally, and should resolve through teamwork rather than any single PC's solo brilliance. Use the terrain (failing road, venting gas, unstable ceiling) as an active participant in the fight, not just flavor text. However Denbei's personal fate resolves, the mining company's negligence should remain unambiguously true and unresolved — that's not a problem this encounter fixes.

sections.heading: What the Ground Remembers
sections.readAloud: However the ridge ends, the Hollow wakes up the next morning to a quieter version of the same town. Kessler Street's sinkhole is still a hole. The noodle shop is still open. Nobody's forgotten anything, and nothing about the mining company's old paperwork has changed just because four provisional heroes had a very bad night on a ridge above town.
sections.body:
• Amagai's report on the incident will, characteristically, undersell it by several orders of magnitude. She'll also, in private, tell the party this is the first time in three years she's trusted anyone enough to write "handled" instead of "contained."
• Sato's monitoring data becomes a real lever if the party pursued it — enough for a formal Commission inquiry into Kessler Mining's liability practices, slow-moving and unglamorous, exactly the kind of institutional win this campaign's world actually offers instead of a clean villain-defeated ending.
• Denbei's brother's name is still on the memorial boulder. So, eventually, is a small addition — the town's own choice, not the party's to make, about how to remember what he did and why.
• The placement continues. There is, per the Commission's own numbers, no shortage of other small towns exactly like this one, and Tidewell Point's stipend just got renewed for another year.
sections.dmNote: Give the epilogue real space — this campaign earns a quiet ending, not a triumphant one. If you want a hook into a longer game afterward, the clean options are: (1) the Commission inquiry into Kessler Mining drags the party into testimony and a bigger institutional fight, (2) the Rural Placement Program reassigns the four of them together again next season, having noticed the match worked, or (3) simply end it here — this campaign was built to stand alone.

closing.label: Villain Presence — Chapter 3
closing.body: Denbei is the entire villain presence of this campaign — there is no larger organization, no hidden mastermind, no sequel-hook faction waiting in the wings unless the DM wants one. That's deliberate: this campaign is about a specific, human-scale failure of a system that's supposed to protect people, seen through four provisional students who were never meant to be the ones who noticed it.

appendix.heading: Chozen's Contingency Binder
appendix.body: By Chapter 2 he's stopped pretending it's a notebook and started calling it what it is. It has tabs. Ren asks, without fail, whether "the volcano plan" is still in there. It is. Chozen has updated it twice.

appendix.heading: Izuto's Toolkit
appendix.body: The leg-maintenance ritual continues, and somewhere around Chapter 2 the others start quietly noticing when he's overdue for it — a full session without the telltale click of the wrench means something's wrong and he hasn't said so yet.

appendix.heading: Kazama's Scar
appendix.body: Never explained unless the DM chooses to spend it — Collapse Point in Chapter 3 is the natural place, but it's just as valid to leave it as an open, unresolved detail the players never get a clean answer to. Either is in-genre.

appendix.heading: Ren's Tally
appendix.body: The running count of 'things that should have stopped me' continues from whatever number your table's Season 1 campaign ended it on, or starts fresh at zero if this is a standalone game. Miller's Ridge should add at least one entry. He will not explain the methodology if asked.

appendix.heading: Amagai's Corkboard
appendix.body: Every piece of evidence, every laminated map, every one-page contingency summary Chozen produces unprompted ends up pinned here. By the campaign's end it is an genuinely useful investigation board that nobody consciously decided to build.

campaigns.title: Class 1-A — First Term
campaigns.tagline: A self-contained U.A. opening, told fresh — Ruin, and only Ruin.
campaigns.tone: A standalone premade campaign for Class 1-A's first term at U.A. — original incidents throughout, built to run with almost no prep. The exam, the dorm, the training grounds, and the first real fight are all written fresh for this module rather than borrowed from any other run of this class. Ruin is the only villain faction that exists in this telling; no other movement, group, or name gets airtime. Treat this as its own closed loop — a table can run it without any knowledge of, or connection to, any other Class 1-A campaign.

background.heading: Premise
background.body: Twenty hopefuls make it into U.A.'s Hero Course. Five of them are played at your table; the rest are a live, reactive cast the DM runs alongside them. First Term covers one exam, one settling-in stretch, one friendly rivalry event, and one real fight — start to finish, self-contained, Level 1 to Level 6.

background.heading: Overview
background.body:
Chapter 1 — The Entrance Exam (Level 1, 2-3 sessions): a staged rescue exam is how this class of twenty meets each other for the first time.
Chapter 2 — Twenty Strangers, One Dorm (Levels 2-3, 3 sessions): move-in chaos and downtime, closing on a friendly 3v3 bracket at the training grounds.
Chapter 3 — First Contact (Levels 3-4, 3 sessions): a field placement puts the class in front of Ruin for the first time.
Chapter 4 — Escalation (Levels 4-6, 4 sessions): a set-piece confrontation with a Ruin cell closes the campaign out.

background.heading: Adventure Hooks
background.body:
No external hook is needed to get these five involved — they're classmates, and the campaign is built to make that proximity do the work. The exam seats them near each other by chance, the dorm keeps them near each other by design, and the 3v3 bracket in Chapter 2 is deliberately structured so no team is all-PC, forcing early contact with the wider cast too.

If your table wants a firmer push toward the five bonding specifically, two easy levers: seat them at the same lunch table from Chapter 1 onward without comment, or have Oshiro assign dorm rooms alphabetically by quirk category — either justifies proximity without requiring a session zero conversation about it.

background.heading: The Cast
background.body: Five PCs: Ren Suzuki (Beams From His Eyes — ranged striker), Kazama Kenji (Steel — frontline tank), Chozen Tadachi (Stress — escalating striker), Izuto Kutsu (Engine — rapid striker), and Zaro Brando (Warp Gate — mobility and battlefield control). Full sheets are in the character library. The remaining sixteen named students round out the class and should show up in downtime scenes whether or not a player is behind them — treat their roster entries (quirk, role, personality) as the baseline; the specific scenes below are new.

background.heading: The Villains
background.body: Ruin is the campaign's only antagonist faction. Every villain scene in First Term is written as a functional placeholder — enough to run tonight, deliberately light on deep characterization so a later rework of Ruin's specific members and motives can drop straight in without disturbing anything else here.

background.heading: Running This Module
background.body: Milestone leveling, not tracked XP — the class opens at Level 1 and closes at Level 6, with each chapter calling out its milestone at the end. Written for a full class in fiction but mechanically sized for four to six seated players; scale enemy counts and HP to your actual table. If your table is smaller than five, let players double up on secondary students in scenes their own PC isn't central to.

chapters.title: The Entrance Exam
chapters.intro: Twenty strangers, one exam, no time to plan. This is the first time any of them see what the others can actually do, and the exam doesn't pause for introductions. Two adults get real introductions this chapter — the exam proctor, who they'll likely never see again, and their new homeroom teacher, who they will.
chapters.dmNote: Run the exam as one long, fast scene rather than a dungeon crawl. Give each PC a single clean spotlight beat during the chaos; everyone else is color. Voice the two named NPCs distinctly from the start — Kessho flat and administrative, Oshiro huge and economical with words — since the tonal contrast between them is doing some of the world-building here.
chapters.milestone: Clearing the exam and surviving the first night in the dorm completes First Term's opening milestone — Level 2.

sections.heading: Arrival
sections.readAloud:
The campus gate doesn't look like much — that's deliberate. Past it, the grounds sprawl out further than the brochure photos suggested, and every person walking by is a stranger you're about to be evaluated alongside.

A woman with a clipboard and a lanyard is trying, without much success, to get roughly a hundred nervous teenagers into anything resembling a line. She gives up around the third attempt and just starts reading names off a list instead.
sections.body:
No pre-established groupings. Let players introduce their PCs to each other and a few named NPCs in the crowd before anything starts. This is the only quiet scene in the chapter.

Use this window to plant a couple of small, specific first impressions among the wider applicant pool, even for names that won't matter later — it sells the scale of the exam. Aikawa is already loudly volunteering to help a proctor carry equipment nobody asked her to touch. Somewhere in the crowd, a small purple haze drifts past two people before they clock that someone's actually inside it.

aside.label: First Meeting — Proctor Kessho Naoto
aside.body:
The woman with the clipboard. Mid-thirties, sharp bob haircut, exam-staff windbreaker two sizes too big for her. Talks fast, flat, and entirely without warmth — she has done this briefing several hundred times today already and it shows.

Once the applicants are roughly gathered, she doesn't bother with a welcome speech:

KESSHO: "You'll find prop civilians and combat drones inside. Prop civilians don't move. Drones do. Don't hit the prop civilians — I don't care how convincing they look, they cost more than your tuition. That's it. That's the whole briefing."

She checks her clipboard, doesn't wait for questions, and walks off toward the observation platform. She will not appear again this chapter — the exam starts on nobody's cue but its own.

sections.heading: The Exam Begins
sections.tag: No warning · Medium encounter, scales to table
sections.readAloud: There's no countdown. One moment it's a staged city block and Kessho's clipboard disappearing through a side door; the next, a support column buckles and something mechanical is pulling itself out of the rubble that used to be a wall. Somewhere behind you, someone screams — it might be a recording. You can't tell yet, and that's the point.
sections.body:
A staged rescue-and-combat scenario: unstable structures, a handful of low-tier combat drones standing in for villains, mannequin civilians to extract. Scale enemies to your table (base statline: HP = 12 + 3×level, AC 11, +3 to hit, 1d6 damage). Everyone scatters and improvises — there's no assigned strategy going in, and most of the applicant pool is running in different directions at once.

Give each PC one clean beat:
• Ren drops a mannequin "villain" drone at range before it's even finished powering up — nobody clocked he'd fired until the drone was already sparking on the ground.
• Kazama plants himself between a falling support beam and two other candidates and just... doesn't move.
• Chozen's Stress ticks up on its own the moment the first drone opens fire — it isn't waiting for him to decide whether this counts as a threat.
• Izuto's legs kick in for one explosive burst to close a gap nobody else could, then immediately start recalculating for the next one.
• Zaro is already through a doorway that was, a second ago, still on fire, having placed her exit before anyone knew there'd be a fire.

Drop in a few unclaimed applicants doing visibly dramatic things in the background too — a kid freezing a puddle into a ramp, someone else just screaming and running the wrong way — to sell that this is a hundred-person exam, not a five-person one.
sections.developments: The exam closes on a single larger drone that singles out whoever's scored highest so far — a scenario nobody can solve alone. However this resolves, it's the first time this specific group of five has had to actually rely on each other rather than just being in the same place at the same time.
sections.dmNote: This finale isn't meant to be soloable. If a PC tries, let it go visibly wrong before help arrives — not lethal, just a clear lesson. If the table wants a quick line of villain-side flavor mid-fight, one of the low-tier drones has a scuffed marking under its chassis that doesn't match U.A.'s exam inventory. Nobody in the moment has time to notice.

aside.label: Villain Thread — Ruin (placeholder)
aside.body: Nothing from Ruin touches the exam directly. If your table wants a single early seed: the unmarked drone above is logged afterward as watching from an odd angle, filed as another department's equipment. It wasn't.

sections.heading: Results Night
sections.readAloud: Results go up that evening, posted as a group pass — nobody failed alone, and nobody carried it alone either. Before anyone's fully processed that, the door to the common room opens without a knock, and it takes a second for the room to register just how much of the doorway the person filling it takes up.
sections.body: First night in the dorm is short, loud, and a little shell-shocked; treat it as the first scene where this actually starts to feel like a class instead of twenty separate applicants. This is also where the class meets its homeroom teacher for the first time — give this its own few minutes, not a rushed aside.
sections.dmNote: Close the chapter on this scene, not the drone fight. Give it a few minutes before cutting to Chapter 2.

aside.label: First Meeting — Oshiro Daikichi (Homeroom Teacher)
aside.body:
6'4" and built like a wall. Cropped dark hair going grey at the temples. A suit that's visibly been repaired more than once, in ways that suggest the damage wasn't from sitting at a desk. He looks like he's seen everything twice and was unimpressed both times.

He doesn't introduce himself with any ceremony. He has a list, and he starts reading it — last names only, no exceptions, ever:

OSHIRO: "Suzuki."
REN: "...Here."
OSHIRO: "Good. Kutsu."

He works through all twenty names this way, flat and quick, never raising his voice, never needing to. When he's done, he closes the folder.

OSHIRO: "I'm Oshiro. Homeroom, and combat training. You start figuring out who you actually are tomorrow at seven. Get some sleep — today doesn't count as an excuse."

He leaves the same way he arrived: no fanfare, door closing behind him before anyone thinks to ask a follow-up question. Play him as gruff and economical with words throughout the campaign, not cold — he simply doesn't perform warmth, he demonstrates it, and this early he hasn't had a reason to yet.

chapters.title: Twenty Strangers, One Dorm
chapters.intro: No villains this chapter. This is where the class turns into a class — downtime scenes that build the ensemble the rest of the campaign runs on — closing with a friendly 3v3 rivalry event at the training grounds, run by a homeroom teacher the class is still getting the measure of.
chapters.dmNote: Run the first two sessions loosely, picking from the beats below as they fit rather than scripting them in order. The 3v3 event in session three is the chapter's actual set piece and deserves a full session. Oshiro reappears here — he's already been introduced, so play him consistent with Chapter 1 rather than re-establishing him.
chapters.milestone: Finishing the 3v3 event and settling into a working routine completes this chapter's milestone — Level 3.

sections.heading: Move-In
sections.body:
Pure character chaos, no combat. Suggested beats — invent freely, and let players propose their own. Each comes with a line of dialogue to voice directly, so the classmate doesn't just exist as a description:

• NAKAYA EMARI turns the common room lights into an impromptu strobe demonstration mid-argument, "to make a point about circuit safety." The breaker disagrees. Nakaya, delighted rather than chastened: "See? That's exactly the kind of surge I was talking about!"

• MASAHATA SHIKOJI is quietly ranking everyone's exam performance in a notebook he insists isn't a ranking system. Cornered about it: "It's a personal reference document. For my own use. That I update daily. And might mention out loud sometimes."

• Something ZARO BRANDO was holding vanishes into her fog mid-conversation and turns up in an entirely different room an hour later. Asked how: "I don't always know either. I just know it comes back."

• AIKAWA SAKUME fixes a door that wasn't broken before she started fixing it. It is now broken in a new and different way. She's already moved on to the next thing before anyone can point this out.

• SAMITSU HINSEI wins three consecutive rounds of a card game without ever explaining his method. Pressed on it, all he offers is a small, unreadable smile and, "Play your hand."
sections.dmNote: This chapter exists to generate new, table-specific texture — don't be precious about the suggested beats above if players want to build their own. Full sheets for these and every other classmate are in the character library if a player wants to dig deeper into someone they've bonded with.

sections.heading: The Common Room
sections.body:
First real contact with the parallel hero-course class happens here or nearby — a shared meal schedule, a hallway run-in, nothing hostile yet. Use this scene to let each PC form or deepen a bond with one NPC classmate of the player's choosing.

Sample exchange if a PC pushes past small talk with MASAHATA about his notebook:

PC: "So where do I land on the list?"
MASAHATA: (visibly pleased to be asked) "Currently unranked pending additional data. Come find me after the 3v3. I'll have numbers."

Sample exchange with NAKAYA, if a PC asks what she's actually excited about:

NAKAYA: "Everything! I mean it. I've never been somewhere this many things could go wrong at once. It's incredible."
sections.dmNote: Keep this scene short if the table's eager to get to the 3v3 — it's connective tissue, not a set piece.

sections.heading: The 3v3 Trials
sections.tag: Friendly bracket · full session · Easy, no lasting stakes
sections.readAloud:
Team assignments go up on the practice-ground board with no explanation for how they were picked. Oshiro's already out past the treeline by the time anyone thinks to ask him about it.

OSHIRO: "Three a team. Elimination by tag, HP to zero, or a three-second hold. Nothing lethal. Figure out why the teams are what they are. You've got until sundown."
sections.body:
A single-elimination 3v3 bracket at the training grounds, mixed PCs and NPC classmates, deliberately split so no single team stacks every PC. NPC opponents use a simplified statline: HP = 15 + 3×level, AC 11 + DEX mod, +3 to hit, 1d6 + STR/DEX damage.

Let each PC's round show off what makes them dangerous:
• Ren's team wins a round from twenty feet back — he ends it before the other team closes the distance they were counting on.
• Kazama eats a combo meant for a teammate and keeps standing.
• Chozen's team wins on accumulated pressure — nothing about round one looks dangerous, round four is a different story.
• Izuto reads an opponent's pattern by round two and has an answer for it by round three.
• Zaro's team wins by controlling where the fight happens rather than winning any single exchange.

Between rounds, Oshiro calls penalties flat and without elaboration — "Out." — and offers exactly one sentence of feedback to anyone who brings him a genuine post-match read on what went wrong. Anyone who doesn't ask gets nothing, which is itself information.
sections.developments: Purely friendly — no lasting stakes beyond pride and a couple of new rivalries worth remembering for later chapters.
sections.treasure: Bragging rights, an extended curfew for the winning team, and a real look at how these five operate together — worth remembering going into Chapter 3.
sections.dmNote: Last purely fun set piece before Ruin enters the story. Let it stay light. If you want a closing beat: Oshiro watches the whole bracket without comment and leaves the moment the last match ends — no debrief, no speech. That's deliberate; he says plenty when it matters and nothing when it doesn't.

chapters.title: First Contact
chapters.intro: The first placement outside U.A.'s walls, and the first time Ruin stops being a rumor and becomes something the class has actually stood in front of. Keep the villain content here light and functional — it's built to be reskinned later, not a deep character study yet. The mentor NPC the class works under this chapter, by contrast, is worth playing fully — he's the class's throughline for the rest of the campaign.
chapters.dmNote: Treat every Ruin NPC in this chapter as a role, not a personality — don't over-invest in backstory that a later rework pass will just replace. Ohta, on the other hand, should feel like a real person from his first line.
chapters.milestone: Surviving First Contact and reporting back completes this chapter's milestone — Level 4.

sections.heading: Field Placement
sections.readAloud: The agency office is smaller than any of you expected, and louder — someone's radio is going in the back, a coffee machine is mid-cycle, and a broad-shouldered man in a half-zipped agency jacket looks up from a stack of paperwork like he's doing the math on five students at once.
sections.body: A day assisting a local agency — no established name is load-bearing here, reskin freely. Mostly administrative on purpose: this is the calm before the chapter's real encounter.

aside.label: First Meeting — Ohta Renji ("Palisade")
aside.body:
Late thirties, broad through the shoulders, a beard he clearly forgets to trim on a schedule. His agency jacket has a faded emblem — a stone wall, cracked but standing — half peeling off the shoulder. Quirk: Bastion, an Emitter ability that lets him raise short-lived barriers of hardened stone from any surface he's touching. He built a career on getting between people and the thing about to hit them.

He doesn't do a formal welcome speech. He just waves the five of you toward the back room without looking fully up from his paperwork:

OHTA: "Five of you. Good — means somebody upstairs actually read my request this time. Filing's through there, coffee's the good stuff if you don't touch the machine's start button twice, and if the phone rings before I get to it, just take a name and number, don't promise anybody anything."

He finally looks up properly, gives the group an actual once-over.

OHTA: "First placement, right? Don't worry about looking useful. Just don't look for trouble. It tends to find people who go looking."

Play him warm, a little dry, and sharper than his easygoing manner suggests — he clocks details about the class faster than he lets on, and it'll show later in this chapter's debrief.

sections.heading: Ruin Shows Its Face
sections.readAloud:
Two figures have a shopkeeper backed against his own storefront when the class turns the corner. Neither of them has clocked the students yet.

A wiry man with a shaved head is doing the talking, cracking his knuckles between sentences like punctuation. "Pay the toll or find somewhere else to sell your fruit," he's saying, bored, like he's said it a hundred times today. Behind him, a broad-shouldered woman says nothing at all — her forearms have a rough, stone-grey texture, sleeves cut away deliberately to show them off.
sections.body:
Two Ruin members shaking down a shopkeeper. Simplified stats — Member A (the talker): HP 15, AC 12, +3 to hit, 1d8 damage. Member B (hardened skin, braced): HP 30, AC 15 (resistant to bludgeoning/piercing while braced), +4 to hit, 1d10 damage. This should feel winnable but real — the class's first fight against people genuinely trying to hurt someone, not a drone or a sparring partner.

If a PC calls out a challenge before the fight breaks out, the talker's response is dismissive rather than scared: "Kids in costumes. Great. Exactly what this was missing." That changes fast once the fight actually starts.
sections.developments: However the fight resolves, let at least one of the two get away or otherwise not be fully accounted for — that loose thread is what Chapter 4 pulls on.
sections.treasure: Recognition from the agency and, if the class thinks to ask, one usable lead from whoever's subdued: a location, a schedule, a name overheard — pick whichever hook best launches Chapter 4.
sections.dmNote: Keep this strictly street-level. No named Ruin leadership here — that's what makes Chapter 4's escalation land.

aside.label: Villain Thread — Ruin (placeholder)
aside.body: Fill in specifics once your Ruin rework is finalized. For now, the one detail worth keeping regardless of how the faction ends up written: whoever gets away is clearly more afraid of being identified than of the students themselves.

sections.heading: What They Didn't Say
sections.readAloud:
Ohta's debrief is calmer than the fight was, and more unsettling for it. He listens to the whole account without interrupting, then sets down his coffee like he's deciding how much to say.

OHTA: "That corner's had trouble before. Not this exact trouble, but trouble that rhymes with it. I've filed three reports about that stretch of street in the last two months and gotten back exactly nothing."

He doesn't elaborate further, catching himself.

OHTA: "Look — good work today, genuinely. Just... keep your eyes open around here. I'll let you know if I hear anything worth knowing."
sections.body: Someone at this agency is clearly tracking more than one street corner, and isn't ready to say how much yet.
sections.dmNote: This is a hook scene, not a reveal. Give the class enough to know Ruin is bigger than one encounter without answering how big — save that for Chapter 4. If a PC pushes Ohta directly on what he's not saying, he deflects honestly rather than lying: "I don't have enough to hand you something real yet. When I do, you'll hear it from me first." He means it.

chapters.title: Escalation
chapters.intro: The thread from Chapter 3 pulls tight. First Term's climax is a real confrontation with Ruin, built as a set piece that closes the campaign out with a win that costs something.
chapters.dmNote: Build this chapter around whichever specific hook your table pulled from Chapter 3 — the beats below are a scaffold, not a script, so they can flex to fit. Ohta can reasonably show up again here if your table wants a familiar face in the investigation stretch — he's earned the continuity.
chapters.milestone: Closing out the confrontation with Ruin completes First Term — Level 6.

sections.heading: The Warning Signs
sections.body:
The class follows up on whatever lead came out of Chapter 3. Keep this to a single session — the goal is arriving at one real location with real stakes, not solving a mystery.

If the class goes back to Ohta for help tracking the lead, he's willing but blunt about his limits:

OHTA: "I can point you at a building. I can't officially send you into it — that's not a 'my agency doesn't want the paperwork' thing, that's a 'you're still students' thing. Whatever you do with the address is on you."
sections.developments: Whatever the class finds should point clearly at a single confrontation rather than spinning off new open threads. First Term is closing out, not seeding a second season.

sections.heading: Confrontation
sections.readAloud:
Whatever this place used to be, it isn't anymore. Ruin's already inside — and for once, they look as surprised to see the class as the class is to see them.

Someone steps out from the group to meet you first. Tall, unnervingly still until the moment they're not. Their voice doesn't rise even a little.

"You're a long way from home, kids."
sections.body: A larger set-piece fight against a Ruin cell: 2-3 rank-and-file members plus one tougher enforcer as the chapter's boss (an intentional placeholder slot — reskin freely once your Ruin rework lands). Suggested boss statline: HP 60, AC 16, +5 to hit, 2d8+3 damage, one signature ability of your choosing.
sections.developments: The class wins the room, but let it cost something — a PC takes a real hit, a lead from Chapter 4's investigation is put at risk, or the enforcer gets away rather than being captured. First Term should end on a win that doesn't feel entirely clean.
sections.treasure: Public recognition, a step up in standing with whichever agency the class has been working with, and confirmation that Ruin runs deeper than anything fought so far — a clean seed for whatever comes next.
sections.dmNote: The highest-stakes fight in the module. Make sure all five PCs get a genuine spotlight moment before it resolves — Zaro cutting off an escape route with a pre-placed portal, Chozen's accumulated damage finally maxing out, Ren landing the shot that closes the fight from across the room, Kazama tanking the hit that would have ended the fight badly, Izuto landing the read that turns it.

aside.label: Villain Thread — Ruin (placeholder)
aside.body: The named enforcer here is intentionally undeveloped — swap in whichever Ruin figure fits once the faction rework lands. What should carry forward regardless: they escape, or are captured but are clearly not the top of the chain, leaving Ruin's actual leadership untouched.

sections.heading: First Term's End
sections.readAloud:
A quiet scene back in the dorm. Nothing about the room looks different, but the class does. Oshiro's already heard — of course he has — and he doesn't make a thing of it, just catches a couple of PCs in the hallway on his way past.

OSHIRO: "Heard you handled yourselves." (a pause, the closest thing to approval he offers) "Get some rest. Same time tomorrow."

He's gone before anyone can turn that into a longer conversation.
sections.body: The city is very slightly more complicated than it was in Chapter 1, and for the first time, that fact belongs to all five of them equally.
sections.dmNote: Land this soft — the previous section was the climax; this is the exhale, not another beat of tension.

appendix.heading: Minimal-Prep Checklist
appendix.body: Before each session you need three things: which section(s) you're running, the enemy statlines for any encounter in it, and one hook from the previous session to open on. NPC names, downtime color, and Ruin specifics can all be invented or reskinned at the table without breaking anything downstream — that's by design.

appendix.heading: Reskinning Ruin
appendix.body: Every Ruin scene in this module works as written using generic roles (a member, an enforcer). Once a fuller Ruin writeup is ready, drop named members and motives directly into Chapters 3 and 4's asides — nothing else in the campaign needs to change to accommodate it.

appendix.heading: Cast at a Glance
appendix.body:
PCs — Ren Suzuki (Beams From His Eyes, ranged striker), Kazama Kenji (Steel, frontline tank), Chozen Tadachi (Stress, escalating striker), Izuto Kutsu (Engine, rapid striker), Zaro Brando (Warp Gate, mobility/control).

Frequently-featured classmates — Nakaya Emari (Element/Lightning, giggly and a menace to common-room electronics), Masahata Shikoji (Water Gun, arrogant, keeps informal rankings of everyone), Aikawa Sakume (Iron Claws, loud, first to volunteer for anything), Samitsu Hinsei (Dupli-Arms, quiet tank, unreadable at cards).

Full sheets for all twenty students are in the character library — this list is just what you need at the table without alt-tabbing.

Adults — Kessho Naoto (exam proctor, brisk and administrative, one-scene appearance in Chapter 1), Oshiro Daikichi (homeroom teacher, hero name Warden, Aftershock quirk; huge, gruff, calls everyone by last name, never raises his voice), Ohta Renji (hero name Palisade, Bastion quirk; runs the Chapter 3-4 field placement, warm but sharper than he lets on).

appendix.heading: Random Encounters (Optional)
appendix.body:
Drop one of these into Chapter 2 or Chapter 4's downtime/investigation beats if a session runs short or the table wants an extra scene. Roll a d6 or pick whichever fits:

1. A first-year Support Course student mistakes a PC for a teacher and asks them to sign off on a gear request.
2. An upperclassman offers to overhaul a PC's gear or costume — for a favor to be named later.
3. A classmate challenges a PC to an unofficial, off-the-books sparring match before curfew.
4. A local reporter is waiting outside the gates hoping for a comment about the exam or the Sports rumor mill.
5. A minor Quirk mishap in the common room needs handling quietly before a teacher notices.
6. A late supply delivery gets misrouted to the wrong dorm, and someone has to fix it after curfew.
